🇦🇺 Australian Representative ITU Elite World Championships Indigenous Pioneer
His story

The athlete

From the Great Lakes
to the world stage.

Growing up in Forster on the New South Wales coast, Brett Lee discovered triathlon as a teenager and quickly showed a gift that would take him further than anyone from his community had gone before in the sport.

In 2004 Brett won the Australian All-Schools Triathlon Championships and the New Zealand All-Schools Triathlon Championships.

By 2004, Brett was competing at the ITU World Championships in Madeira, Portugal — finishing 9th in the world in the Junior Sprint division. He was named Australian Junior Triathlete of the Year, received the Paterson Sports Person of the Year Award presented personally by Prime Minister John Howard, and won the Deadly Award for Most Promising Indigenous New Talent in Sport.

In 2005 he went further still — becoming the first Australian to win the Trans Tasman Junior Elite Sprint Championship, captaining the NSW team at Nationals, and qualifying first for the Australian squad for the ITU World Championships in Japan.

Just prior to the World Championships in Japan, Brett had a serious accident where he rode his bike into the back of a parked car. He received serious neck and throat injuries and was on life support for a week in Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney.

Remarkably, he recovered sufficiently to compete at the World Championships in Japan three months later. Brett's courage and fortitude was recognised by the awarding of the NSW Institute of Sports Ian Thorpe Award for Recovering Under Adverse and Duress Circumstances.

He was the first Indigenous Australian to represent Australia internationally in the sport of triathlon.

The man

Reconnecting with
Country.

Brett was adopted by a non-Aboriginal couple as a newborn and grew up in Bourke, Orange, Bourke, Kempsey and Forster in New South Wales. At 14, he began the journey of reconnecting with his Ngiyampaa heritage — a thread that would run through everything that followed.

His name Pirritu is the Ngiyampaa word for Brett. Choosing it as his artist name was not just a creative decision — it was a statement of identity, belonging, and pride in where he comes from.

Beyond his music, Pirritu volunteers with the Ngiyampaa Language Project, working to make the language more accessible and to deepen his own understanding of Country and culture.

The musician

From injury
to a new song.

When injury forced Brett away from elite sport, he turned inward — teaching himself music theory and beginning a journey just as remarkable as his athletic career. Performing as Pirritu, he makes folk music that carries the weight of his personal story: adoption, identity, culture, and belonging.

Based in Melbourne, his music has earned him back-to-back nominations for the Archie Roach Foundation Award for Emerging Talent at the Music Victoria Awards.

Press & Recognition

A name that made
headlines.

Great Lakes Advocate  ·  April 28, 2004

PM honours Forster athlete

Prime Minister John Howard personally presented Brett with the Paterson Sports Citizen of the Year Award in Raymond Terrace. Brett gifted the PM a limited-edition "Bretto" team shirt produced to fund his World Championship campaign in Portugal.

National  ·  2004

Australian Indigenous Award — Most Promising New Talent in Sport

Recognised nationally as the most exciting young Indigenous sporting talent in the country. Brett's rise through the sport was pioneering — the first of his people to carry the Australian flag in triathlon on the international stage.

Music Victoria Awards  ·  2022 & 2023

Archie Roach Foundation Award — Emerging Talent

Nominated in consecutive years for one of Victorian music's most meaningful honours — named for the legendary Archie Roach — Pirritu has earned recognition as one of the most compelling new voices in Australian folk and Indigenous music.
